description: Branch prediction hint __builtin_expect through LOOMORA_LIKELY / LOOMORA_UNLIKELY (used in core/src/c_api.cpp); the fallback is the plain condition, with identical behaviour.
reason: Compilers without __builtin_expect (MSVC, unknown compilers) take the fallback. No platform of validation/platforms/ takes it: the three of them build with GCC (MinGW-w64 GCC 13 for Windows, GCC 13 for Linux), which has __builtin_expect.

description: [[nodiscard]] on the internal C++ functions is_eol, eol_warning, abi_version and build_compiler through LOOMORA_NODISCARD; the fallback is an empty attribute, so the discarded-result warning is lost but behaviour is identical.
min_compiler: C++17 mode (__cplusplus >= 201703L or _MSVC_LANG >= 201703L): gcc 7, clang 3.9, msvc 19.11 (VS 2017 15.3)
reason: The backend is built as strict C++11 on every Legacy target (and as C++14 where MSVC or the CMake clang/MSVC STL combination imposes it), so those builds take the fallback; only a build in C++17 mode or later uses [[nodiscard]]. All three platform records take it: their builds are strict C++11 (cpp_std of the deliverable records).

description: Dark theme of the Windows Legacy UI (ui/legacy/windows-win32/dynfeatures.cpp): when the user's "apps use light theme" setting (HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Themes\Personalize\AppsUseLightTheme, read through advapi32 loaded at run time) is 0 and no high contrast scheme is on, the window and its controls use dark colours (text 14:1 on the background) and, through dwmapi!DwmSetWindowAttribute when it exists, a dark title bar. The fallback is the colours of the system, which every Windows version applies by itself.
min_compiler: not a compiler feature: looked up at run time, any compiler; needs the AppsUseLightTheme setting (Windows 10, build 1607 or 1703 to verify, and Windows 11); a dark title bar needs Windows 10 version 1809 or later
reason: Windows 2000 to 8.1 have no dark theme setting for applications: the value is missing, the feature is skipped and "dark-mode" is added to disabled_features of the probe record; the greeting stays legible with the system colours. Exercised on Windows 11 only (light and dark). Taken by windows-2000-x86 (Windows 2000 build 2195: "dark-mode" in disabled_features of its probe records, validation/evidence/first-trial/windows-2000-x86/); not taken by windows-11-x64 (disabled_features empty in 40 probe runs).

description: DPI awareness of the Windows Legacy UI: SetProcessDPIAware (user32) is looked up at run time and called before the window exists, the layout and the GUI font are then scaled to the system DPI. The fallback is not to call it.
min_compiler: not a compiler feature: looked up at run time, any compiler; SetProcessDPIAware exists since Windows Vista
reason: Windows 2000 and XP do not export SetProcessDPIAware: the call is skipped and "dpi-awareness" is added to disabled_features. Nothing is lost there, those systems do not virtualize the DPI, so the program already sees the real one (the layout is still scaled by it). Only the system level is requested: a window moved to a monitor of another DPI is stretched by the system. Exercised on Windows 11 at 100% only. Taken by windows-2000-x86 ("dpi-awareness" in disabled_features of its probe records, validation/evidence/first-trial/windows-2000-x86/); not taken by windows-11-x64 (disabled_features empty in 40 probe runs).

description: High contrast query of the Windows Legacy UI: SystemParametersInfoW(SPI_GETHIGHCONTRAST), looked up at run time in user32; when a high contrast scheme is on, the dark theme of the UI is not applied and the system colours stay. The fallback is to assume no high contrast scheme.
min_compiler: not a compiler feature: looked up at run time, any compiler; SPI_GETHIGHCONTRAST is available since Windows 2000
reason: Every Windows of the range (2000 to 11) is believed to export SystemParametersInfoW with this action, so the skip is a defensive path that is not expected to be taken; it is declared because the code can take it. The controls use system colours by default, so a high contrast scheme is respected even without the query. Not exercised with a high contrast scheme on. No platform of validation/platforms/ takes it: SystemParametersInfoW answered on Windows 2000 build 2195 and on Windows 11 (the probe records do not list it).

description: Peak memory of the Windows Legacy UI in probe mode: GetProcessMemoryInfo (PeakWorkingSetSize) from psapi.dll, loaded from the system directory at run time. The fallback is peak_rss_kb = -1 in loomora_probe_record, which the record shows as null.
min_compiler: not a compiler feature: looked up at run time, any compiler; psapi.dll is part of Windows 2000 and later
reason: The measure is best effort (ui-contract.md): when psapi.dll or the function is absent the probe record has a null peak_rss_kb and "peak-memory" in disabled_features. Not expected on Windows 2000 SP4 and later (psapi.dll ships with it, to verify on a real system); the skip path was not exercised. No platform of validation/platforms/ takes it: psapi.dll answered on Windows 2000 build 2195 and on Windows 11 (the probe records do not list it).

description: Link-time shim of KERNEL32!GetThreadId in the Windows 2000 executables (ui/legacy/windows-win32/getthreadid_shim.cpp, linked into loomora.exe and loomora_selftest.exe only by the toolchain of the Windows 2000 build). It satisfies the reference of libgcc's gthr-win32.o inside the executable so that the import table does not name GetThreadId, and calls the real function at run time when kernel32 has it. The path without the fallback, which every other target takes, is the system's own GetThreadId through the import table.
min_compiler: not a compiler feature: the CMake variable LOOMORA_TARGET_WIN2000, set by cmake/toolchains/mingw-w64-win2000-i686.cmake and read by ui/legacy/windows-win32/CMakeLists.txt and core/tests/CMakeLists.txt (a compile-time switch for a target-wide limit); needed with MinGW-w64 GCC 13 and its win32 thread model, a libgcc that does not reference GetThreadId would not need it
reason: GetThreadId exists since Windows Vista and Windows Server 2003 SP1, so Windows 2000 and Windows XP x86 do not export it and their loader refuses an executable whose import table names it (adr/0002). Before adr/0004 the shim was keyed on 32-bit MinGW builds; it is now keyed on the Windows 2000 toolchain only, so the x64 build (XP x64 and later have the function) and any other 32-bit build keep the real import. Verified 2026-11-13 on the Windows 2000 build 2195 VM: loomora_selftest, built with the shim by the Windows 2000 toolchain, prints "all passed" (exit 0), while the control built without it is still refused by the loader (exit 128); the run is not stored (CLAUDE.md: a re-run); the first proof is in validation/evidence/selftest-no-iostream/windows-2000-x86/.

description: Output of core/tests/selftest.cpp through std::fputs of <cstdio> instead of std::cout of <iostream>, selected by the compile definition LOOMORA_AVOID_IOSTREAM. The iostream initialisation of a static libstdc++ pulls the thread-support code of libgcc (gthr-win32-cond.o) into the program, which imports Vista-only KERNEL32 functions (InitializeConditionVariable, SleepConditionVariableCS, WakeConditionVariable, WakeAllConditionVariable). Behaviour is identical, only the stream differs.
min_compiler: not a compiler feature: a compile definition set by both MinGW-w64 toolchain files (cmake/toolchains/mingw-w64-win2000-i686.cmake and mingw-w64-win-x86_64.cmake, floors older than Windows Vista) and by tools/guest/build_selftest.sh; GCC 13 with a static libstdc++ and the win32 thread model. The host build (clang with the MSVC STL) and the Linux builds do not define it and use <iostream>.
reason: Both Windows toolchains target a floor older than Vista: Windows 2000 (i686) and Windows XP x64 (x86_64), and the x86_64 selftest with <iostream> was measured to import the same four Vista-only functions (tools/check_imports.py --arch x64, 2026-11-13), so it would not load on XP x64 either. windows-11-x64 is listed because its deliverable is the x86_64 build of that toolchain, whose selftest takes the fallback although Windows 11 itself would run <iostream>; there is no platform record for XP x64. std::printf is not an alternative: MinGW-w64 maps it to __mingw_vfprintf, which imports msvcrt _lock and _unlock, absent from the allowlist. Verified 2026-11-13: the selftest built with the fallback prints "all passed" on the Windows 2000 VM and on Windows 11 (x86_64 build), and has no import outside the allowlist of its architecture; the host builds (clang on Windows, g++ on Linux) use <iostream> and pass ctest.

description: Font of the controls of the Windows Legacy UI (ui/legacy/windows-win32/dynfeatures.cpp): the message font of the system, SystemParametersInfoW(SPI_GETNONCLIENTMETRICS).lfMessageFont looked up at run time in user32 (Segoe UI 9 pt on Windows Vista and later, the older size of NONCLIENTMETRICS is tried when the Vista one is refused). The fallback is the stock DEFAULT_GUI_FONT (MS Shell Dlg 8 pt) scaled to the system DPI by the program.
min_compiler: not a compiler feature: looked up at run time, any compiler; SPI_GETNONCLIENTMETRICS is available since Windows 2000
reason: Every Windows of the range (2000 to 11) is believed to answer SPI_GETNONCLIENTMETRICS, so the skip is a defensive path that is not expected to be taken; it is declared because the code can take it, and "message-font" is then added to disabled_features. Before adr/0004 the stock GUI font was used on every Windows, which is the font of Windows 2000 and looks dated on Vista and later. Not exercised: the skip path, and any DPI above 100%. On the Windows 2000 VM and on Windows 11 the call succeeds (no "message-font" in disabled_features of 15 + 30 probe runs); the controls get MS Sans Serif 8 pt there and Segoe UI 9 pt (lfHeight -12 at 96 DPI) on Windows 11.

description: Visual styles of the EDIT and STATIC controls of the Windows Legacy UI: the manifest (ui/legacy/windows-win32/loomora.manifest) depends on Common Controls 6, which the loader of Windows XP and later honours. The fallback is the classic look of the controls, with no change of behaviour.
min_compiler: not a compiler feature and not a C++ macro (the name identifies the manifest dependency): read by the loader of Windows XP and later, ignored by Windows 2000, which has no side-by-side assemblies
reason: Windows 2000 ignores manifests altogether, so its controls keep the classic look, which is the only look it has; the manifest was kept empty of every entry before adr/0004 only because of that system. Windows 11 draws the themed EDIT (light and dark, both executables) and Windows 2000 the classic one, the 15 vectors passing on both (screenshots in validation/evidence/adr-0004/). Not run on Windows XP to 8.1.

description: C++ runtime of the GTK Modern UI executable (ui/modern/linux-gtk3): the meson option static_cxx_runtime (default false) links libstdc++ and libgcc statically. The default is the distribution's libstdc++.so.6 and libgcc_s.so.1.
min_compiler: not a compiler feature and not a C++ macro (the name identifies the meson option static_cxx_runtime): the default needs libstdc++.so.6 from GCC 5 or later (GLIBCXX_3.4.21) on the target distribution; the option is for one that has none or an older one
reason: ADR 0001 rule 4 links the C++ runtime statically where the platform has none or an old one. No platform of validation/platforms/ is in that case, so the default is dynamic; see adr/0004 for the sizes and symbol versions measured. Measured on Ubuntu 24.04 (GCC 13.3, glibc 2.39), same objects linked both ways by tools/trials/linux-ubuntu-24.04-x86_64/gtk-floor-and-runtime-check.sh: the dynamic default is 53,736 bytes (the size of the meson build) and asks for GLIBC_2.34 and GLIBCXX_3.4.21; the static runtime is 296,952 bytes (296,848 in the earlier meson build) and asks for GLIBC_2.38, because libstdc++.a of this toolchain was built against a newer glibc. On this platform the static link is therefore the more restrictive choice, not the safer one.

description: Alignment of the text of the wrapped end-of-life warning label of the Linux Modern UI (ui/modern/linux-gtk3/main.c, set_label_text_start): gtk_label_set_xalign(label, 0) when the GTK headers are 3.16 or later (every GTK 4 header too). The fallback is gtk_misc_set_alignment(label, 0, 0.5) of the 3.10 API (GtkMisc, deprecated in 3.14 and removed in GTK 4); the text is left-aligned the same way in both, mirrored in a right-to-left locale.
min_compiler: gtk 3.16 headers: GTK_CHECK_VERSION(3, 16, 0) and GDK_VERSION_MAX_ALLOWED >= GDK_VERSION_3_16 (ui/modern/linux-gtk3/gtk_compat.h); always on with GTK 4 headers. Not a compiler feature.
reason: Headers older than GTK 3.16 (a distribution of 2014 or 2015 such as Ubuntu 14.04, GTK 3.10) and the floor build (-Dgtk_floor=true, GDK_VERSION_MAX_ALLOWED pinned to 3.10) take the GtkMisc fallback. No platform of validation/platforms/ takes it: linux-ubuntu-24.04-x86_64 has GTK 3.24.41 headers and takes the modern path. The fallback path was compiled and run only through the floor build on that platform (GTK 3.24 runtime, not a real GTK 3.10); a real GTK 3.10 system was not tried.

description: Scrollbar of the greeting of the Linux Modern UI (ui/modern/linux-gtk3/main.c, create_scroller): gtk_scrolled_window_set_overlay_scrolling(scroller, FALSE) when the GTK headers are 3.16 or later (every GTK 4 header too), so that the scrollbar stays visible beside the text of a long greeting. The fallback is not to call it: GTK 3.10 has no overlay scrollbars, its scrollbar is always visible and takes room, which is what the call restores on newer GTK (the default there is an overlay hidden until the pointer moves).
min_compiler: gtk 3.16 headers: GTK_CHECK_VERSION(3, 16, 0) and GDK_VERSION_MAX_ALLOWED >= GDK_VERSION_3_16 (ui/modern/linux-gtk3/gtk_compat.h); always on with GTK 4 headers. Not a compiler feature.
reason: Headers older than GTK 3.16 and the floor build take the fallback; the greeting then has the scrollbar of the toolkit in use (always visible on a real 3.10, an overlay hidden until hover on a 3.16+ runtime). No platform of validation/platforms/ takes it: linux-ubuntu-24.04-x86_64 builds with GTK 3.24.41 headers and takes the modern path. Visible difference measured with screenshots in WSLg: the floor build shows no scrollbar on a 1,000-character greeting, the default build shows one.

description: GTK 4 branch of the Linux Modern UI (ui/modern/linux-gtk3/main.c, gtk_compat.h, gtk_compat.c), selected at build time by the meson option -Dgtk_api=4 (dependency gtk4 instead of gtk+-3.0) and in the code by GTK_MAJOR_VERSION >= 4 (LOOMORA_GTK4): the same window content with the GTK 4 API (gtk_window_set_child, gtk_box_append, margins, GtkEditable text, a GMainLoop, the first display taken from the after-paint signal of the frame clock). The fallback is the GTK 3 UI, which is the default build. Differences of the GTK 4 branch: the end-of-life warning is a plain box (warning icon, text, close button) because GtkInfoBar is deprecated since 4.10 and has no replacement, so it has no warning background; the display time of the probe is the end of the first painted frame instead of the first draw.
min_compiler: gtk 4.0 headers (GTK_MAJOR_VERSION >= 4), built with -Dgtk_api=4; tried with GTK 4.14.5 and GCC 13.3. Not a compiler feature.
reason: GTK 4 is opt-in (-Dgtk_api=3 is the default), so every deliverable takes the GTK 3 path, linux-ubuntu-24.04-x86_64 included even though its libgtk-4-dev is installed: the GTK 3 UI is the one of all the trials, the floor of the UI is GTK 3.10 and a system without GTK 4 stays served. On GTK 4.14.5 in WSLg the branch builds without a warning, passes the 15 reference vectors and the probe checks; the Mesa EGL warnings it prints on standard error under WSLg ("libEGL warning" lines, 134 bytes on the X11 backend, 265 on the default Wayland backend) come from the OpenGL renderer, not from the UI; on the Wayland backend they disappear with GSK_RENDERER=cairo or LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1. The GTK 4 build has no trial verdict.

description: Text path of the Linux Legacy UI (ui/legacy/linux-xlib/main.c, xftdl.c). The normal path draws with client-side fonts through libXft and fontconfig, both opened at RUN TIME with dlopen (nothing links against them): fontconfig's sorted list for "sans-serif" gives, for each code point, the first installed font that has it (per-code-point fallback), so Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Hebrew, Arabic, CJK, symbols and emoji are real glyphs in the greeting and in the input line. THIS FALLBACK is the older path, taken ONLY on a system where libXft.so.2 or libfontconfig.so.1 cannot be loaded (or no font can be opened, or the test switch LOOMORA_XLIB_NO_XFT is set): the core X11 font "fixed" through XDrawString (ISO 8859-1 font) or XDrawString16 (font whose CHARSET_REGISTRY / CHARSET_ENCODING is ISO10646 / 1); a character it cannot draw (a code point the font lacks, a control character, a code point above U+FFFF, an invalid byte) is drawn as '?' and the UI adds "glyph-substitution" to disabled_features of the probe line; the greeting and the probe record are unchanged, only the picture is. Every other system uses the Xft path. LIMITS OF THE XFT PATH (accepted by the owner, they apply wherever it runs, they are not this fallback): NO TEXT SHAPING AND NO BIDIRECTIONAL LAYOUT, Xft draws the code points one after the other in logical order, left to right. Arabic letters are therefore drawn in their isolated forms and left to right, Hebrew and Arabic words appear visually reversed, a combining mark is drawn at the pen position of the character before it only when its font gives it a zero advance, a ZWJ sequence (a family emoji, a flag) is drawn as its separate components, an Indic conjunct is not formed; the invisible format characters (U+200B..U+200F, U+202A..U+202E, U+2060..U+2064, variation selectors, U+034F, U+00AD, U+180B..U+180D, U+FEFF) take no room and draw nothing. A code point NO installed font has (and a control character) is drawn as an empty box drawn by the UI (a tofu), never as '?', and the UI adds "missing-glyph" to disabled_features of the probe line. Emoji come from the first font of the list that has them: on the measured system U+1F600 is a monochrome outline from DejaVu Sans, while the emoji DejaVu Sans lacks (the fox, the three components of a family emoji) are drawn in colour from Noto Color Emoji.
min_compiler: not a compiler feature and not a C macro (the name identifies the run-time test fontset_open in xftdl.c, whose failure selects the core-font path and is reported as the disabled feature glyph-substitution): the Xft path needs libXft.so.2 and libfontconfig.so.1 loadable by dlopen (libXft 2.x with its Xrender and FreeType dependencies, fontconfig 2.x), an X server with the RENDER extension and at least one installed font with Latin letters; the core-font path needs an X server whose core font "fixed" is ISO 10646-1 to draw more than Latin-1
reason: A system without libXft (a very old distribution, a minimal one, a 32-bit userland without the 32-bit libXft) can only draw with core X11 fonts, which have no shaping, no combining marks, no bidirectional layout, no colour and no fallback font, so what they lack cannot be drawn. PLATFORMS THAT TAKE IT: none of the platform records of this repository (platform_ids is empty on purpose: validate_records.py only accepts ids that have a platform record, and the executables concerned are recorded under the generic ids linux-i686 and linux-manylinux2010-i686 until T087). Measured: (1) the i686 executable on Ubuntu 24.04 (WSLg, x86_64 kernel), where only libx11-dev:i386 / libx11-6:i386 are installed and there is no 32-bit libXft or fontconfig: dlopen fails, the UI draws with the core font, "fixed" is -Misc-Fixed-Medium-R-SemiCondensed--13-120-75-75-C-60-ISO8859-1 (the server lists 6 fonts, none ISO 10646), so only U+0020..U+00FF is drawn: Latin-1 text (Zoé, élève) is drawn, the euro sign, Greek, Cyrillic, Hebrew, Arabic, CJK and emoji are '?', and "glyph-substitution" is in the probe line (validation/evidence/xlib-unicode-manylinux/linux-ubuntu-24.04-x86_64/); both i686 executables (native and manylinux2010) were run that way, 15 of 15 reference vectors pass with them. (2) the x86_64 executables on the same machine find libXft and fontconfig and take the Xft path: they do NOT take this fallback (linux-ubuntu-24.04-x86_64 no longer lists it), the same screenshots show the real glyphs; the core-font path was also forced on them with LOOMORA_XLIB_NO_XFT (the same behaviour as the i686 one). On the Xft path (WSLg, libXft 2.3.6) the screenshots show: Latin with accents, the euro sign, Greek, Cyrillic and CJK as real glyphs, Hebrew and Arabic as real glyphs but in logical order from left to right (Hebrew visually reversed, Arabic letters isolated and not joined, as accepted), an e followed by U+0301 drawn as one accented letter (the font gives the mark a zero advance), a ZWJ family drawn as three separate colour emoji, the zero width space drawn as nothing, and two empty boxes for U+0378 and U+10FFFD. The ISO 10646-1 path (XDrawString16) was exercised only by forcing it on an 8-bit font in a test copy earlier (the earlier evidence, kept as history: validation/evidence/linux-legacy-xlib/ shows the '?' pictures that this change supersedes); it was NOT run with a real ISO 10646-1 core font. NOT tested: a real old distribution without libXft, a 32-bit system with a 32-bit libXft (the 32-bit Xft path was never run, only the 64-bit one), other X servers and distributions, any other font set than the one of this machine (429 fontconfig fonts, Noto and DejaVu), any text shaping or bidirectional text (none exists by decision).

description: C++ runtime of the Linux Legacy UI executable (ui/legacy/linux-xlib/Makefile): libstdc++ and libgcc are linked STATICALLY (STATIC_CXX=1) only for the manylinux2010 container build, the old-glibc baseline target (python tools/build.py linux legacy --toolchain manylinux2010, images quay.io/pypa/manylinux2010_x86_64 and _i686), so that the executable needs no libstdc++.so.6 / libgcc_s.so.1 on a CentOS 6 style system. The native build (the modern path, every other platform) uses the default STATIC_CXX=0: the distribution's own libstdc++ and libgcc_s, linked dynamically.
min_compiler: not a compiler feature and not a C++ macro (the name identifies the Makefile variable STATIC_CXX, default 0, set to 1 by tools/build.py for the container build): the static variant needs the GCC of the manylinux2010 image (devtoolset-8, GCC 8.3.1, whose static libstdc++ was built for glibc 2.12); the dynamic variant (the default) needs libstdc++.so.6 from the GCC that built it (GLIBCXX_3.4.21 for GCC 5 and later) on the target system
reason: The Linux Legacy floor is glibc 2.12 (CentOS 6, Debian 6), whose libstdc++ is far older than what a C++11 backend needs, so the static runtime is the case of that floor and only of that floor (ADR 0004, finding 13: it used to be applied to every build). PLATFORMS THAT TAKE IT: the two manylinux2010 container builds, recorded under the generic ids linux-manylinux2010-x86_64 and linux-manylinux2010-i686 (no platform record yet, T087; platform_ids is empty because validate_records.py only accepts ids that have a platform record). Measured with the same sources: native x86_64 on Ubuntu 24.04 (gcc 13.3, glibc 2.39): dynamic (default) 67,280 bytes, NEEDED libX11.so.6, libstdc++.so.6, libgcc_s.so.1, libc.so.6, highest GLIBC_2.34 / GLIBCXX_3.4.21 / CXXABI_1.3; static (STATIC_CXX=1) 306,136 bytes, highest GLIBC_2.38 and no GLIBCXX (the libstdc++.a of that toolchain was built against a recent glibc), so a static native build would only make the executable bigger and no older. In the manylinux2010 container (GCC 8.3.1, glibc 2.12, STATIC_CXX=1): x86_64 253,424 bytes, i686 1,086,080 bytes (the 32-bit static libstdc++ pulls in the verbose terminate handler and with it the demangler and iostream, the 64-bit one does not), both with NEEDED only libX11.so.6, libdl.so.2, libc.so.6 and the loader, highest GLIBC symbol version GLIBC_2.7 and no GLIBCXX / CXXABI / GCC version node (objdump -T, the container log is out/linux-legacy-manylinux2010/<arch>/container-build-log.txt and the numbers are in the deliverable notes), which is within the glibc 2.12 baseline. This is a symbol-version check: the executables were run only on Ubuntu 24.04 (WSLg), not on glibc 2.12 or any 2010-era distribution.
